title.text: Hoover School on Olive Street, Westminster 1944

textContent.text: The NAACP wanted to desegregate schools, meaning they wanted to end school segregation. In 1945, the NAACP assisted the Mendez family in a lawsuit to desegregate schools in Westminster, California. The school district made Mexican-American students, such as Sylvia Mendez, attend a poorly funded "Mexican" school rather than a better-funded school closer to her home.

Mendez's lawyer used testimony from scientists and educational experts to support school desegregation. Mendez won the case and was allowed to attend the school. Just two months after Mendez's 1947 victory, California's governor signed a law to end all racial segregation in California's schools.

Since this was a state law, rather than a federal one, it did not affect the rest of the country. It was rare for a state government to independently desegregate its own schools. Governors in the Jim Crow South supported segregation and would not voluntarily desegregate schools.

pieces.text: The 1896

Supreme Court decision allowed states to create "separate but equal" schools for African American students, but Black families argued that their schools were underfunded and inferior. With the NAACP's support, families in several states filed lawsuits against their local school districts to challenge segregation in schools. Oliver Brown filed a lawsuit because his eight-year-old daughter, Linda, had to attend a Black school twenty-one blocks away from their house rather than a white school just seven blocks away. Brown's lawsuit was combined with four others when the Supreme Court considered them.
In 1954, the Supreme Court's

decision stated that segregation in public schools was unconstitutional. It said that even if segregated schools had equal buildings, funding, and qualified teachers, being forced to attend segregated schools would still make African American students feel inferior to white students. It also said school segregation "may affect their hearts and minds in a way unlikely ever to be undone." Therefore, the Court argued that segregated schools could never be equal and that the idea of "separate but equal" had no place in education.

textContent.text: The NAACP wanted to desegregate schools, meaning they wanted to end school segregation. In 1945, the NAACP assisted the Mendez family in a lawsuit to desegregate schools in Westminster, California. The school district made Mexican-American students, such as Sylvia Mendez, attend a poorly funded "Mexican" school rather than a better-funded school closer to her home.

Mendez's lawyer used testimony from scientists and educational experts to support school desegregation. Mendez won the case and was allowed to attend the school. Just two months after Mendez's 1947 victory, California's governor signed a law to end all racial segregation in California's schools.

Since this was a state law, rather than a federal one, it did not affect the rest of the country. It was rare for a state government to independently desegregate its own schools. Governors in the Jim Crow South supported segregation and would not voluntarily desegregate schools.

title.text: Hoover School on Olive Street, Westminster 1944

textContent.text: The NAACP wanted to desegregate schools, meaning they wanted to end school segregation. In 1945, the NAACP assisted the Mendez family in a lawsuit to desegregate schools in Westminster, California. The school district made Mexican-American students, such as Sylvia Mendez, attend a poorly funded "Mexican" school rather than a better-funded school closer to her home.

Mendez's lawyer used testimony from scientists and educational experts to support school desegregation. Mendez won the case and was allowed to attend the school. Just two months after Mendez's 1947 victory, California's governor signed a law to end all racial segregation in California's schools.

Since this was a state law, rather than a federal one, it did not affect the rest of the country. It was rare for a state government to independently desegregate its own schools. Governors in the Jim Crow South supported segregation and would not voluntarily desegregate schools.

contents.text: In 1955, the story of a 14-year-old Black child named Emmett Till brought national attention to racial violence in the South. While on a trip from Chicago to visit family in Mississippi, Emmett Till was accused of flirting with an older white woman. He was kidnapped, beaten, and killed. contents.text: In 1955, the story of a 14-year-old Black child named Emmett Till brought national attention to racial violence in the South. While on a trip from Chicago to visit family in Mississippi, Emmett Till was accused of flirting with an older white woman. He was kidnapped, beaten, and killed. Two white men were tried for Till's murder but were found not guilty by an all-white jury. Four months later, the men publicly admitted to kidnapping and killing Till.

Till's death left a lasting impact on many African American youth. In 2011, civil rights activists Dorie Ann Ladner and Joyce Ladner, who were teenagers in 1955, recalled their reactions to Till's murder. Read an excerpt from their interview. Then answer the question below.

contents.text: In 1955, the story of a 14-year-old Black child named Emmett Till brought national attention to racial violence in the South. While on a trip from Chicago to visit family in Mississippi, Emmett Till was accused of flirting with an older white woman. He was kidnapped, beaten, and killed. Two white men were tried for Till's murder but were found not guilty by an all-white jury. Four months later, the men publicly admitted to kidnapping and killing Till.

Till's death left a lasting impact on many African American youth. In 2011, civil rights activists Dorie Ann Ladner and Joyce Ladner, who were teenagers in 1955, recalled their reactions to Till's murder. Read an excerpt from their interview. Then answer the question below.

title.text: Emmett Louis Till

pieces.text: [Emmett Till]…that's when a light bulb went off. Why aren't [his killers] being punished? That's when I went on my quest to try to understand the whole legal system and equal rights and justice under the law.…
It was like a

call for action and that when we got older we were going to [respond to] his death. I mean, I can remember feeling that so strongly. I remember clipping [the local newspaper] every time there was an article about the Emmett Till case and the trial, and I kept a scrapbook.
